cues.text: Hey, welcome back.
Imagine holding a flat frame in a breeze.
Face it into the breeze and plenty of air crosses its opening.
Turn it edge on and much less crosses.
Electric flux uses a similar geometric idea, although electric field is not a
flowing substance.
For a flat surface in a uniform field, flux equals field magnitude times area
times the cosine of the angle between the field and the area vector.
The area vector points perpendicular to the surface.
That angle is not automatically the angle to the plane of the surface.
If a question gives the angle to the plane, convert it to the angle to the normal.
Let's take a field of two hundred newtons per coulomb and area zero point zero
three square meters.
If the field makes sixty degrees with the chosen normal, flux is three newton
square meters per coulomb.
At ninety degrees to the normal, the field lies along the plane and flux is
zero.
Reversing the normal reverses the sign.
For a curved surface or varying field, split the area into tiny patches and add
the field dot area contributions, which becomes a surface integral.
An open surface has a chosen normal convention.
A closed surface uses outward normals.
Flux is a scalar, but its sign carries the direction of the field through that
oriented surface.
Now close the surface completely, like an imaginary box around a region.
Gauss's law says its total outward electric flux equals the net enclosed charge
divided by vacuum permittivity.
Add enclosed charges algebraically.
An outside charge does not contribute to the net enclosed charge, even though
its field can be strong on the surface.
In the flux integral, the electric field is the total field from all sources.
For an external source, field entering and leaving makes zero net closed
surface flux.
This is the trap to remember: zero enclosed charge means zero net flux, not
necessarily zero field.
Put an empty box in a uniform field.
Field passes through it; flux entering one side cancels flux leaving the other.
Let's enclose plus two nanocoulombs and minus half a nanocoulomb.
Net charge is one point five nanocoulombs.
Divide by eight point eight five times ten to the minus twelve, giving about
one hundred and sixty nine point five newton square meters per coulomb.
Move an outside charge around and this total stays the same, provided no charge
crosses the boundary.
But individual surface fields change.
Gauss's law applies to any closed surface.
To turn it into a simple formula for field strength, however, we need enough
symmetry to know the field direction and how its magnitude varies over our
chosen surface.
The law and the shortcut are not the same thing.
Consider an isolated thin spherical shell with charge distributed uniformly
over its surface.
Symmetry tells us that field must be radial, with the same magnitude everywhere
at a fixed distance from the center.
Choose a concentric imaginary sphere of radius r.
The field is along its normal, so the flux becomes field times four pi r
squared.
Outside the shell, the enclosed charge is the entire shell charge.
Gauss's law gives the same outside field as a point charge at the center.
Inside the shell, enclosed charge is zero.
Because the spherical symmetry still makes the field constant and radial on a
concentric sphere, the field is zero.
This last conclusion uses symmetry, not zero flux alone.
For shell charge two nanocoulombs and shell radius ten centimeters, at twenty
centimeters from the center the field is four hundred and fifty newtons per
coulomb, using the Coulomb constant nine times ten to the ninth.
At five centimeters inside, the field is zero.
These results assume an isolated, uniformly charged thin shell.
Don't substitute them for a solid insulating sphere with charge spread
throughout its volume.
For that different model, enclosed charge inside grows as r cubed, and field
grows linearly with r.
Nor should you assume an arbitrary shell remains uniformly charged when
external sources distort its distribution.
Always name the distribution before choosing the surface.
For an ideal infinitely long uniformly charged straight line, a sphere is an
awkward choice.
A coaxial cylinder matches the symmetry.
Let the cylinder have radius r and length ell.
Field points radially away from a positive line and has constant magnitude on
the curved side.
On the flat end caps, field lies along the surface rather than through it, so
their flux is zero.
The side contributes field times two pi r ell.
Enclosed charge is linear charge density lambda times ell.
Substitute into Gauss's law and the cylinder length cancels.
Field is lambda divided by two pi epsilon zero r.
Unlike a point charge, this field falls as one over r, not one over r squared.
Let's use lambda equal to two nanocoulombs per meter and r equal
to ten centimeters. With k equal to nine times ten to the ninth, the equivalent relation two k
lambda divided by r gives three hundred and sixty newtons per coulomb.
Double r and the field becomes one hundred and eighty, not ninety.
The imaginary cylinder is a calculation surface; it is not a physical
conducting tube.
For a finite charged wire, the infinite line approximation is most useful near
its central region when perpendicular distance is much smaller than the
distance to either end.
Without that approximate symmetry, the end cap argument and simple formula
cannot be used blindly.
For an ideal infinite nonconducting sheet with uniform surface charge density,
symmetry gives equal field magnitudes on both sides, perpendicular to the sheet.
Choose a short imaginary pillbox crossing it.
No field crosses the curved side.
Both flat faces contribute outward flux, so the total is two E A.
The charge inside is sigma times A, and field becomes sigma divided by twice
vacuum permittivity.
That factor of two is easy to lose.
If sigma is one point seven seven times ten to the minus nine coulombs per
square meter and epsilon zero is eight point eight five times ten to the minus
twelve, field magnitude is one hundred newtons per coulomb on either side.
It does not decrease with distance in this infinite sheet model.
A finite sheet needs distances small compared with its lateral size and points
away from edges for this approximation.
Now contrast a conducting surface in electrostatic equilibrium.
Field within the conducting material is zero.
A tiny pillbox straddling its surface gets flux only through the outside face,
giving the field just outside as local surface charge density divided by
epsilon zero.
Here sigma means the charge density on that particular conductor face, not
automatically the total charge divided by both faces of a slab.
Our closing routine is simple: identify symmetry, choose a closed surface,
write every flux contribution, count enclosed charge, and only then solve for
the field.
